haz mat.here: Dad is joking. He says he will call the team that cleans up dangerous things.

woo hoo.example: When Freddy first saw it, he shouted, “Woo-hoo!”
woo hoo.here: He shouts “Woo-hoo!” — a happy shout — when he first sees it.

air conditioning.meaning: a machine that makes room air cold
air conditioning.example: I suddenly felt cold, like the air-conditioning had been cranked up real high.
air conditioning.here: The room feels cold, as if the machine that makes room air cold is on high.

budget bustin.meaning: using up too much money; breaking the spending plan
budget bustin.here: The papers use up too much money. They break the plan for spending.

polka dotted.example: “I like your hat,” she tells Penny, who is holding Doodle closely and wearing a blue polka-dotted hat with a red feather.
polka dotted.here: The hat is blue with small round spots.

sandy haired.example: The driver—a sandy-haired guy who’s been on this route for a couple of years—beeped once more, then rumbled on.
sandy haired.here: The driver is a man with yellow-brown hair.

heigh ho.meaning: a happy shout from an old horse-rider song
heigh ho.here: It is a happy shout from an old song about a horse rider.

take up.meaning: to fill or use time or space
take up.example: mostly it was simply something to do that took up time and got me out of the house.
take up.here: Here school was something to do that took up time — filled her hours.

move up and on.meaning: to go to a higher grade and keep going, like other classes do
move up and on.example: We never seem to move up and on like other classes.
move up and on.here: Here Melody's class never seems to move up and on — go to a higher grade — like other classes.

come up for air.meaning: to come back up to the top of the water to breathe
come up for air.example: He takes a deep breath, like a swimmer coming up for air.
come up for air.here: Here Willy is like a swimmer coming up for air — coming up to breathe.

call on.meaning: (of a teacher) to ask a student to answer
call on.example: And even if she were to call on me, what then?
call on.here: Here Melody wishes the teacher would call on her — ask her to answer.

run on.meaning: to work or go by using something
run on.example: A system that runs on grits instead of good sense.
run on.here: Here Mrs. Shannon jokes that the school system runs on grits — works by means of grits — instead of good sense.

on top of one's list.meaning: as the most important thing; first
on top of one's list.here: Here Mrs. Shannon put getting an aide for Melody way up on top of her list — as her first, most important thing.

deals and wheels.here: Here Catherine says she will be Melody's 'deals and wheels' — a playful flip of 'wheels and deals,' taking care of everything.

in honor of.meaning: to celebrate something or show it respect
in honor of.example: Orange ones, of course, in honor of Halloween, while she read poems about pumpkins and ghosts.
in honor of.here: Here they ate orange Popsicles in honor of Halloween — to celebrate it.

what is it with.meaning: what is wrong with them; why do they act this way
what is it with.example: re jealous of me or something.
what is it with.here: Here Melody asks, 'What is it with those two?' — what is wrong with Claire and Molly?

mixed up.example: d come over to me that I got all mixed up.
mixed up.here: Here Melody got all mixed up — confused — when Rose came to talk to her.

long division.meaning: a way of dividing big numbers, with many written steps
long division.here: Here Melody wonders when she will ever get to long division — the hard dividing done in math class.

out sick.meaning: not at school or work because of illness
out sick.example: Mrs. Shannon was out sick that day, so I sat quietly...
out sick.here: Here Mrs. Shannon was out sick — not at school because she was ill.

stay put.meaning: to stay where you are; not to move
stay put.example: s gonna snow next week. Stay put for another month!
stay put.here: Here Melody tells the little flowers to stay put — stay where they are — for another month.

be done with.here: Here Mom asks if they are done with winter — finished with the cold.

soak up.meaning: to take in fully, like a dry sponge takes in water
soak up.example: Nobody seems to be amazed that Penny is soaking up and learning thousands of words.
soak up.here: Here Penny is soaking up thousands of words — taking them in fast.

get off.meaning: to get down from or leave a bus, train, or plane; (of work) to finish and go home.
get off.here: Here Chuck got off early — finished work early.

car seat.meaning: a small, safe seat for a child in a car
car seat.example: she gets to ride in her little car seat in the back.
car seat.here: Here Penny rides in her little car seat in the back of the car.

have other ideas.meaning: to have different plans; to not agree
have other ideas.here: Here Mom has other ideas — different plans — when Penny runs to Dad.

set of eyes.here: Here Mom says she needs four sets of eyes — four people watching — with Penny.

all you can eat.meaning: where you may eat as much as you want
all you can eat.here: Here Linguini's has all-you-can-eat spaghetti — eat as much as you want.

walking distance.here: Here the restaurant is walking distance — close enough to walk to — from the studio.

night out.meaning: an evening spent having fun away from home
night out.example: These kids deserve a special night out!
night out.here: Here the kids deserve a special night out — a fun evening away from home.

be so kind as to.meaning: a polite way to ask someone to do something
be so kind as to.here: Here Mom asks, 'Would you be so kind as to ask an employee...' — a polite request.

clap someone on the back.here: Here Connor's dad clapped him on the back — patted his back — to show praise.

dig into.example: Conversation slowed down as everybody dug into their meals.
dig into.here: Here everybody dug into their meals — started eating with joy.

pick at.meaning: to eat only very small bits of food
pick at.example: s fish looked a little, well, fishy, as she picked at it with her fork.
pick at.here: Here Mom picked at her fish — ate only very small bits.

cheer up.example: Being reminded of cake and ice cream cheered up Connor.
cheer up.here: Here the thought of cake and ice cream cheered up Connor — made him happy again.

whipped cream.meaning: sweet cream beaten until thick and fluffy, put on sweet foods
whipped cream.example: He smeared whipped cream over his second piece of cake.
whipped cream.here: Here Connor smeared whipped cream — thick, fluffy sweet cream — on his cake.

easy listening.example: she switched the radio to an easy-listening station and turned the volume down low.
easy listening.here: Here Mrs. V switched the radio to an easy-listening station — soft, calm music.

know better than to.meaning: to be wise enough not to do something
know better than to.example: Mrs. V should know better than to say stuff just to make me feel better.
know better than to.here: Here Melody thinks Mrs. V should know better than to say stuff — be wise enough not to say it — just to make her feel better.

i mean it.meaning: I am serious; I am not joking
i mean it.here: Here Mrs. V says 'I mean it, Melody' — she is serious.

beyond one's control.here: Here Mrs. V says some things are beyond our control — we cannot control them.

be the case.meaning: to be true; to be how things are
be the case.here: Here Mrs. V believes Penny being alive is still the case — still true.

fall apart.meaning: to break down completely; to fail
fall apart.example: My whole world would fall apart if something happened to you.
fall apart.here: Here Mrs. V says her whole world would fall apart — break down completely — if something happened to Melody.

picture window.meaning: a very large window in a house
picture window.example: I glanced out of her large picture window and watched the wet branches sway.
picture window.here: Here Melody looked out of the large picture window — the very large window.

one's heart drop.meaning: to suddenly feel fear or sadness
one's heart drop.here: Here Melody's heart dropped — she suddenly felt fear — when Mrs. V cried, 'Oh, no!'

special place in one's heart.here: Here Mrs. V says Melody has a special place in her heart — she deeply loves her.

home run.meaning: (in baseball) a hit that lets the player run all the way home and score
home run.here: Here Willy knows who first hit sixty home runs — sixty scoring hits — in one season.

grown ups.meaning: adults; people who are not children
grown ups.example: the type of music grown-ups think is all kinds of noise

give a shout out.example: And I want to give a special shout-out to Melody, who really helped us secure our victory!
give a shout out.meaning: To speak someone’s name in public in order to praise or thank them.

the twenty fifth hour of one's day.meaning: extra time that does not really exist (a joke about being too busy)
the twenty fifth hour of one's day.here: There is no twenty-fifth hour — she jokes that she has no time.
the twenty fifth hour of one's day.example: "Right. I'll get to potty training tonight—on the twenty-fifth hour of my day!"

do one's share of.meaning: To do or experience a lot of something.
do one's share of.example: I did my own share of tumbling onto that rug.

here's the thing.meaning: Said before telling an important fact.
here's the thing.example: Here’s the thing: I’m ridiculously smart, and I’m pretty sure I have a photographic memory.

be used to.meaning: to be familiar with something already; to be accustomed to it.
be used to.example: Penny was used to things falling off my chair.
be used to.here: Penny was already familiar with things falling; she was used to it.

bite on.meaning: to believe something; to fall for a trick.
bite on.example: I knew he'd bite on that one.

candy cane.meaning: a Christmas candy shaped like a walking stick.
candy cane.example: Hyatt and every teacher after her always let Maria take charge of the green paper cutout candy canes and the purple-striped stars cut from wrapping paper.

come out.meaning: to turn out in a certain way; to become known.
come out.example: It's hard to put my feelings into words that will come out right on my talker.

high five.meaning: slapping your raised hand against someone else's hand to celebrate.
high five.example: He holds his hand up in the air for high fives.

hold one's head high.example: We roll down to the room, and I hold my head high.

honey buns.meaning: a sweet name for a small child.
honey buns.example: ‘Not today, honey buns,’ Mrs. V says firmly.

round of applause.meaning: everyone clapping together at one time.
round of applause.example: Let's all give Melody a round of applause.

special needs.example: The 'special needs' bus, as they call it.

stand out.example: I'll make them stand out, and not in a good way.

talking board.meaning: a board with words or pictures a person points to in order to communicate.
talking board.example: Her ‘talking board’ has just two words on it— yes and no.

weed out.meaning: to remove the weaker ones; to get rid of.
weed out.example: It is designed to be challenging, to weed out the weaker candidates.

wet one's pants.meaning: to lose control of your pee from fear or laughter; here a joke meaning 'can't wait'.
wet one's pants.example: ‘Now read the names before Connor wets his pants!’

take charge.meaning: to take control; to become the leader.
take charge.example: Hyatt and every teacher after her always let Maria take charge of the green paper cutout candy canes and the purple-striped stars cut from wrapping paper.

the minute.example: From the minute she came home from the hospital, she was a really happy baby.

i mean.meaning: words used to explain more clearly what you just said.
i mean.example: We rushed—I mean, ran like track stars.

on a roll.meaning: to keep talking with strong feeling, without stopping.
on a roll.here: Mom was on a roll; she kept talking with strong feeling.

a big deal.example: It's televised and is a really big deal.

at that point.example: I don't know how old the snowman was at that point.

note cards.meaning: small cards with words written on them to help you remember.
note cards.example: When we arrive at Mr. Dimming's room, a group of kids from my history class are already there, whispering together and going over note cards.

have one's nails done.meaning: to have your fingernails painted or cared for.
have one's nails done.example: Even her little fingernails have been done to match.

guitar strumming.meaning: music played by moving fingers across guitar strings.

left handedness.meaning: using your left hand more than your right hand.
left handedness.example: What is 'diplopia'? A. Double vision B. Left-handedness C. A disease of the gums D. A form of cancer.

x ray.meaning: a kind of light that can go through your body; doctors use it to see bones.
x ray.example: They would've needed X-ray vision like Superman to see what was in my head.

high scoring.meaning: getting a lot of points in a game.
high scoring.example: We wait for the next teams to compete, then we'll meet and beat the other high-scoring team and pack our bags for Washington!

highest scoring.meaning: getting the most points in a game.

top scoring.meaning: getting the most points; the best at scoring.
top scoring.example: You are our two top-scoring schools.

set up.meaning: to arrange things so someone is likely to fail.
set up.example: Maybe we're setting her up for failure, and she'll be hurt even worse.

ma ma.example: Penny saying 'ma-ma' and 'da-da' just like the babies on Sesame Street.

paragraphs.context: Words have always swirled around me like snowflakes
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody knows thousands of words, but she cannot speak a single one of them.
paragraphs.simple: Words move around Melody like snowflakes in the air. Each one is pretty and different. But just as she cannot hold a snowflake in her hand without it disappearing, she cannot pick up these words and use them. They melt untouched.

paragraphs.context: Deep within me, words pile up in huge drifts
paragraphs.mainIdea: Inside her head, Melody has mountains of language, but no way to get it out.
paragraphs.simple: Deep inside Melody, words pile up in big drifts, like snow piled up by the wind. She has mountains of phrases and sentences and connected ideas. She has clever expressions, jokes, and love songs. It is all there, ready, inside her head.

paragraphs.context: Country is lemons—not sour, but sugar sweet
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody does not just hear music; she tastes and smells it at the same time.
paragraphs.simple: For some reason, Melody has always loved loud country music, with guitars and songs about broken hearts. For her, country music is lemons. Not sour lemons, but sweet and tangy, like lemon cake icing and cool, fresh lemonade. Lemon, lemon, lemon. She loves it.

paragraphs.context: These things—I call them my “tornado explosions”— are pieces of me
paragraphs.mainIdea: When Melody gets upset, her body moves wildly and she cannot stop it.
paragraphs.simple: Melody calls her worst moments her tornado explosions. All the parts of her body that do not work get wound up into a tight ball. She cannot stop, even though she wants to, and even though she knows she scares people. She loses control of herself. It can get ugly.

paragraphs.context: I didn’t want to be sent away. Was I a burden?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody is afraid that her parents would have an easier life without her.
paragraphs.simple: Melody stares at her mother in fear. She does not want to be sent away to a home for disabled children. For the first time she asks herself: am I a burden, a heavy load that makes life harder for my parents? Maybe it would be easier for them if she were not around. She gulps, and her hands get cold.

paragraphs.context: It’s like I live in a cage with no door
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody feels trapped inside her body, with no way to show people who she really is.
paragraphs.simple: Melody likes all the children in room H-5, and she understands their problems better than anyone. But there is nobody else like her. It feels like she lives in a cage with no door and no key. And she has no way to tell anyone how to get her out.

paragraphs.context: which would you rather be able to do—walk or talk?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. V asks Melody to choose between walking and talking.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. V asks Melody a hard question. If she had to choose only one, which would she rather be able to do: walk, or talk?

paragraphs.context: ‘If I have to go over those letters one more time,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mom explains that Melody screamed because she was bored and pushed too far, not because she was bad.
paragraphs.simple: Mom believes this is what happened to Melody. Melody said to herself, "If I have to go over those letters one more time, I will just scream." And so she did scream. Mom does not blame her, and she asks the teacher if she blames her either.

paragraphs.context: Maybe he was sick and tired of that bowl and that log
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody wonders if the goldfish was as unhappy with his small life as she sometimes is with hers.
paragraphs.simple: Melody wonders if Ollie was really happy in his little world after all. Maybe he was sick and tired of his bowl, his log, and his endless circle. Maybe he just could not stand it anymore. Melody feels that way about her own life sometimes.

paragraphs.context: It was my job to bring a child into the world
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody's mother says it is her own fault that Melody is the way she is: it was her job to bring a healthy baby safely into the world, and she failed.
paragraphs.simple: Melody's mother is crying hard. She says she is the mother, so it was her job to bring a child into the world safely. She thinks she did it wrong. She says every other woman on earth can give birth to a normal baby, so something must be wrong with her.

paragraphs.context: Life sure would be easier if they had only one child—one with working
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody feels bad: she thinks life would be easier for her parents if they had only one child — one whose body works the way it should, like a machine with working parts.
paragraphs.simple: After they stop talking, Melody still feels a little bit bad. She thinks life would be easier for her parents if they had only one child. And that child would be one with a body that works — “working parts,” like the parts of a machine.

paragraphs.context: I wonder if she ever wished she could get a refund for me.
paragraphs.mainIdea: After the story of the broken doll that Mom returned to the store, Melody asks herself a painful question: did Mom ever wish she could “return” her the same way?
paragraphs.simple: Melody told the story of the broken doll. Her mother took the doll back to the store and got her money back. Now Melody wonders: did her mother ever wish she could get her money back for her, too — take her back like a broken toy?

paragraphs.context: if I had somebody to write the words over my head
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody wishes someone could write her thoughts in big bubbles over her head — the way Garfield's words appear in little circles — so people would know what she is thinking.
paragraphs.simple: Garfield is a cat who cannot really talk. His words are written in little circles over his head. Sometimes Melody feels the same way. She wishes someone could write her thoughts in big floating bubbles over her head. Then people would know what she is thinking. She could live with that.

paragraphs.context: It was driving me crazy that I couldn’t tell him about
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody starts to lose control — kicking, with her arms stiff — because she cannot make her father understand that she wants a Big Mac.
paragraphs.simple: Melody can feel she is about to lose control. She starts to kick. Her arms get stiff. It is driving her crazy that she cannot tell her father about a stupid Big Mac. She wants it so much, but she has no way to say it.

paragraphs.context: When I started seeing the colors, I knew she was
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Lovelace plays the piano so well that Melody begins to see colors with the music — forest green, lime green, emerald — which tells her this teacher is really good.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Lovelace sits at the piano and plays “Moon River,” then the theme from a vampire movie. She knows what the kids like. When Melody starts seeing colors — forest green, lime green, emerald — she knows Mrs. Lovelace is good. For Melody, beautiful music comes with colors.

paragraphs.context: Finally, a girl got up out of her seat and walked
paragraphs.mainIdea: Rose — the girl who made an angry face when her friends laughed at kids like Melody — comes to Melody's chair with a smile and tells Melody her name.
paragraphs.simple: At last a girl stands up and walks to Melody's chair. She bends down low and looks Melody in the face. Then she gives a warm smile. It is the girl with long hair — the one who made an angry face at her friends when they laughed. “I’m Rose,” she says in a soft voice.

paragraphs.context: It was the best feeling in the world! I felt like
paragraphs.mainIdea: For the first time in her life, a teacher tells Melody to stop talking because she is talking with a friend in class — and this makes her feel like all the other kids.
paragraphs.simple: Rose finally understands the joke about the jazz music, and they both laugh so hard that Mrs. Lovelace puts a finger to her mouth to tell them to stop talking. No teacher has ever told Melody to stop talking for talking with someone in class. It is the best feeling in the world. She feels like the rest of the kids.

paragraphs.context: Of course I knew, so I raised my hand, but the
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody knows the answer to the teacher's question, but the teacher does not notice her small hand movement — and even if she were called on, she could not speak the answer. It makes her feel terrible.
paragraphs.simple: The teacher asks for the definition of “dignity.” Melody knows it, so she raises her hand. But the teacher does not see the small movement she can make. And even if the teacher called on her, what then? She cannot call out the answers. It is really frustrating.

paragraphs.context: A system that runs on grits instead of good sense
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Shannon says she is sorry: the school has too much paperwork and a slow system that is not smart, but she put getting a helper for Melody at the very top of her list.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Shannon says she is sorry. There is budget-breaking paperwork. The school system “runs on grits instead of good sense” — it is slow and not smart. She is trying to get every H-5 student the services they need. But she put getting a helper for Melody way up on the top of her list. She is hoping for a wonderful school year!

paragraphs.context: I’d gotten an eighty-five, but I was so excited that she’d
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody actually scored 85 — higher than Rose's 75 — but she is so excited that Rose came to talk to her that she points to 5 and then 8 by mistake, so Rose thinks she did badly.
paragraphs.simple: Melody got an 85 on the test. Rose got a 75 and looks sad. Melody is so excited that Rose walked over to her that she gets mixed up. She points to 5 and then 8 on her board. Rose feels sorry for her and says, “Don’t worry. You’ll do better next time.” Rose does this in front of everyone, so Melody cannot tell her the real score.

paragraphs.context: Some people get braces on their teeth. Some get braces on
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. V tells Claire that everyone has something about them that is not quite right: Claire needed braces for her teeth, others need braces for their legs, and some need wheelchairs — so Claire should remember she is lucky.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. V asks Claire why her parents spent good money on braces for her teeth. Her teeth were not quite right. Some people get braces on their teeth. Some get braces on their legs. For others, braces will not work, so they need wheelchairs and walkers. Claire is lucky that only her teeth were messed up. She should remember that.

paragraphs.context: dreaming of the perfect Melody-made computer. First of all, it would
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody dreams of a perfect computer made just for her: it would talk, and it would hold all her words — not just the few pasted on her board.
paragraphs.simple: Melody closes her eyes and tries not to cry. She dreams of the perfect computer made for her. First, it would talk! People would even have to tell her to be quiet! And it would have room to keep all her words — not just the most common ones pasted on her dumb plastic board.

paragraphs.context: the words better, nicer, and cooler just aren’t there. So I
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody's board does not have the words “better,” “nicer,” or “cooler,” so she builds “gooder” from “good” + “E” + “R” — which sounds wrong and makes her feel silly.
paragraphs.simple: Melody points to Rose's computer, then to “me too.” She wants a better computer than Rose's. But her board does not have the words “better,” “nicer,” or “cooler.” So she points to “good,” then to the letters on her board, then to E and R: “Good-er.” It sounds wrong. She feels like a doofus.

paragraphs.context: I want to know how he does ordinary stuff, like eating
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody chooses Stephen Hawking because, like her, he is a grown man who cannot move or speak normally — she wants to know how he takes care of himself in everyday life, like eating, and how he is a dad.
paragraphs.simple: Melody wants to know how Stephen Hawking does everyday things, like eating and drinking. After all, he is a grown man. Does his wife put him on the toilet? He has kids. How does he manage to be a dad? She picks him because his life is like hers.

paragraphs.context: I’ve heard of prescriptions for antibiotics, but for machines? That seems
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody finds it crazy that she needs a doctor's prescription — like for medicine — just to get a talking machine that nobody would want unless they needed it.
paragraphs.simple: Next, they have to ask Melody's doctor to fax in a prescription. Melody has heard of prescriptions for antibiotics — medicine — but a prescription for a machine? That seems crazy to her. Who would ever want this machine unless they needed it? She waits.

paragraphs.context: I realize I have never, ever said any words directly to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody realizes she has never spoken any words directly to her parents before — so she uses the machine to say “I love you” for the first time.
paragraphs.simple: Melody thinks about it and realizes: she has never, ever said any words directly to her parents. So she pushes a couple of buttons. The machine speaks the words she has never been able to say: “I love you.”

paragraphs.context: But Melody has been forced to be silent. She probably has
paragraphs.mainIdea: Miss Gordon explains to Claire that Melody has always had thoughts in her head but was forced to live without speaking — so she probably has a great deal she wants to say.
paragraphs.simple: Miss Gordon answers Claire kindly. Claire has always been able to say whatever comes to her mind. But Melody has been forced to be silent. She probably has mountains of things to say. Melody makes the machine say, “Yes. Yes. Yes.”

paragraphs.context: But at recess I still sit alone. It’s been too cold
paragraphs.mainIdea: Even with Elvira, Melody still sits alone at recess: no girl talks with her about things or asks her to come anywhere — not even Rose.
paragraphs.simple: At recess Melody still sits alone. It is too cold to go outside, so they sit in the hot cafeteria. None of the girls talk with her about funny things boys said. Nobody promises to call her. Nobody asks her to a birthday party or a sleepover. Not even Rose.

paragraphs.context: Dead silence. No cheers. Just looks of disbelief.
paragraphs.mainIdea: When Mr. Dimming says Melody got a perfect score, no one shouts happily — nobody in the room makes a sound because the class cannot believe she won.
paragraphs.simple: When the teacher says Melody got every question right, nobody shows they are happy. The room makes no sound. Everyone looks surprised and full of doubt.

paragraphs.context: On your study plan. You and I are going to practice, prepare, and push.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. V will coach Melody hard for one week so she can try out for the school quiz team.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. V has a plan. For one week, she and Melody will work very hard together. Mrs. V will ask questions, and Melody will answer them. They will study many, many small facts about the world — geography, science, and math — so Melody can try to get on the quiz team.

paragraphs.context: Nobody sent a frantic message to room H-5, wondering why Melody wasn’t in class
paragraphs.mainIdea: Nobody at school noticed that Melody skipped her inclusion classes to study.
paragraphs.simple: Melody stayed in room H-5 all day to study and did not go to her other classes. Nobody sent a worried message to ask where she was. Nobody came to the door to check if she was sick or hurt. Nobody seemed to notice or care at all.

paragraphs.context: People often want to know if I’m sick or if I’m in pain
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody prepared two set answers for people who ask what’s wrong with her: a polite one and a rude one.
paragraphs.simple: People often ask Melody, “What’s wrong with you?” They want to know if she is sick, if she feels pain, or if doctors can fix her body. So she made two ready answers. One answer is polite but long. The other is a little rude, for people who are not kind. For kind people she says she has cerebral palsy, which stops her body but not her mind.

paragraphs.context: that Penny is soaking up and learning thousands of words
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. V says people should not be more amazed by Melody’s learning than by Penny’s — Melody is no different.
paragraphs.simple: Mom says Mrs. V taught Melody thousands of words. Mrs. V answers that nobody is amazed when little Penny learns thousands of words. Penny soaks up new words every day, and nobody thinks it is strange. Melody is the same as Penny. Learning words is normal for both of them.

paragraphs.context: I don’t think it’s appropriate for Melody to be here
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Dimming tells Catherine that Melody should not try out, because the tryout is not just for fun.
paragraphs.simple: Mr. Dimming talks to Catherine, not to Melody. He says he does not think Melody should be in the room. He says this tryout is not a game just for fun. Its purpose is to choose the real school team. He thinks the test will be too hard for her.

paragraphs.context: You will have thirty seconds to record each response
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Dimming explains the test rules: 100 questions, read once, 30 seconds each, answer with a letter.
paragraphs.simple: Mr. Dimming tells the students the rules. There are one hundred questions. He will read each question one time and each answer one time. The students have thirty seconds to write or record each answer. They must write only the letter: A, B, C, D, and sometimes E.

paragraphs.context: Could it be a girl’s heartbeat—pounding too hard?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody jokes that her pounding heart feels like an earthquake on the TV news.
paragraphs.simple: Melody is so excited and nervous that her heart beats very fast and hard. She makes a joke in her head. She pretends a TV weather man is giving an earthquake report. He feels strange shaking coming from a school. The joke is: the “earthquake” is really just her own heartbeat.

paragraphs.context: She got every single question right.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Dimming announces that Melody got a perfect score — every one of the 100 questions right.
paragraphs.simple: Mr. Dimming tells the class that last week he thought Melody’s good score was just luck. But on the real tryout test, she answered every single question correctly. All one hundred. In fifteen years, no student had ever done that. So Melody is on the quiz team.

paragraphs.context: But we weren’t quite a team.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody feels she is not truly part of the team, even though she sits in the same room.
paragraphs.simple: Melody is happy to be on the quiz team. But she feels the truth: there is the team, and there is her, in the same room — yet they are not really one team. The others like that she gets answers right. But she cannot join their fast talk, so she still feels alone.

paragraphs.context: there was no way I could jump in quick enough
paragraphs.mainIdea: The team talks so fast that Melody cannot join the discussion, though she hears and remembers everything.
paragraphs.simple: The happy moment with the team ends fast. The students talk at very high speed. They answer and ask so quickly that Melody cannot type fast enough to join in. She cannot jump into the talk. But she listens carefully, and she remembers everything they say.

paragraphs.context: Everything you see on TV is fake.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody sees that the TV studio is small and fake — nothing like it looks at home.
paragraphs.simple: Melody looks around the TV studio and understands something. Everything on TV is fake. At home, the news seems to show a big window with the whole city behind the reporters. But in the studio it is only a small painting. The desk is small too. Everything looks much bigger on television than it really is.

paragraphs.context: My son is in a wheelchair,” he says with a shrug.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Paul the stage manager understands Melody’s needs because his own son uses a wheelchair.
paragraphs.simple: Paul tells Melody his son Rusty is in a wheelchair too. Paul often builds things to help Rusty. But Paul says Rusty could never do what Melody is about to do. Paul goes down to look Melody in the eye and tells her to show everyone how good she is. Rusty will be watching her on TV.

paragraphs.context: The two teams with the highest scores from all preliminary rounds
paragraphs.mainIdea: The two top-scoring teams will meet in a final quiz-off; the winner goes to Washington and Good Morning America.
paragraphs.simple: Mr. Kingsley explains the last part of the contest. The two teams with the most points from the early rounds will play one final set of questions, called a quiz-off. Points are very important. The winning team becomes the local champion and goes to Washington, D.C. The next morning, the winners will be on national TV, on the show Good Morning America.

paragraphs.context: our team has a total of eighty-one points
paragraphs.mainIdea: Spaulding Street wins round one, 81 to 77, and moves on to the final.
paragraphs.simple: On the last question, Melody answers C: earthquake. She is glad she did not move. Connor, Rose, and Claire get it right too. Two Woodland students answer hurricane, which is wrong. When all points are counted, Melody’s team has eighty-one points and Woodland has seventy-seven. Spaulding Street wins the first round.

paragraphs.context: the team that will represent us in Washington, D.C., this year
paragraphs.mainIdea: Spaulding Street wins the final, 86 to 85, and will go to Washington.
paragraphs.simple: Mr. Kingsley announces the winner. Both teams answered the last math question. Three Perry Valley students got it right, but all four Spaulding Street students got it right. The final score is eighty-six to eighty-five. The winning team is Spaulding Street Elementary School. They will go to Washington, D.C., and may be on Good Morning America.

paragraphs.context: best friends in spite of their differences and members of the winning
paragraphs.mainIdea: On live TV, Claire says she and Melody are best friends who eat lunch together every day — but it is not true.
paragraphs.simple: The reporter runs out of time and ends the interview. She tells the camera that Claire and Melody are two remarkable young women — best friends even though they are different. Melody cannot believe her ears. Claire is not really her friend or her lunch partner. Claire said those nice things on TV, but they are not true.

paragraphs.context: nobody on the team had ever really seen me eat
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody is afraid of the restaurant because no teammate has ever seen her being fed like a baby.
paragraphs.simple: Eating out is usually fine for Melody. But tonight is different. At school she eats with other disabled students, and aides feed them. No one on the quiz team has ever seen her eat — or rather, seen her be fed. She is afraid and does not know what to do when her food sits cold in front of her.

paragraphs.context: yet I’m the one everybody looks at sideways
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody sees what is not fair: Claire was sick in front of everyone, yet people keep looking hard at Melody.
paragraphs.simple: Claire got sick and threw up in a crowded restaurant, in front of everyone. Nobody talks about it. But Melody is the one people look at in a strange, sideways way. Melody sees how unfair this is: Claire did the embarrassing thing, yet Melody gets the stares.

paragraphs.context: but eyes tell the truth. The eyes are cold
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody sees that the other children's kind words are not real; their cold eyes show they are angry that only her picture was in the paper.
paragraphs.simple: Melody says the reaction at school is just what she thought it would be. The children say nice words to her, but their eyes tell the truth. Their eyes are cold, as if Melody had hit the reporter on the head and made her print only Melody's picture.

paragraphs.context: My presence was cute at first, maybe okay for a local competition
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody believes the other children feel she is fine for a small local contest, but on national television she will make the team look bad.
paragraphs.simple: Melody says it is hard to put her feelings into words that will come out right on her talker. She knows the other children are not easy about having her on the team. There is no other way to say it. Having her there was sweet at first, and okay for a small local contest. But the big game on national television is different. She will make them stand out, and not in a good way.

paragraphs.context: The FAA won’t let planes take off in weather like that
paragraphs.mainIdea: The desk agent explains that a snowstorm in the Northeast has stopped flights everywhere, so no plane can take Melody to Washington in time.
paragraphs.simple: The woman says five inches of snow are already on the ground in Boston, and more snow is coming that afternoon farther south. The FAA will not let planes take off in such weather, so the whole flight system is blocked. Planes that were supposed to land here and then fly back east are cancelled, so the afternoon flights cannot leave. She says it is complicated, and she is sorry.

paragraphs.context: The morning started out like crystal, but the day has turned to broken glass.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody says the day began bright and full of hope but has ended in pain, like beautiful crystal turned into broken glass.
paragraphs.simple: Melody just sits there. The morning started out clear and bright, like crystal. But now the day has turned into broken glass — sharp, painful, and ruined.

paragraphs.context: That makes me even crazier because I can’t even do that!
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody is so angry she wants to stomp her feet, but she cannot even move her body to show anger the way other children can.
paragraphs.simple: Melody feels like stomping on something, over and over. That thought makes her even more upset, because she cannot even do that. She cannot even get angry in the way a normal child can.

paragraphs.context: A constant, soaking downpour that laughed at umbrellas and raincoats.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A terrible storm is raging: heavy rain, thunder, lightning, and wind, and the rain is so strong that umbrellas and raincoats are useless.
paragraphs.simple: When Melody woke up that morning, it was raining. There was thunder, lightning, and wind. The rain fell all the time and soaked everything. It was so strong that umbrellas and raincoats were no help at all — it was as if the rain were laughing at them. The air was gray and heavy and full of water. Melody could hear the rain hitting her window hard.

paragraphs.context: Slowly, the big car rolled backward. I felt the soft thud.
paragraphs.mainIdea: As Mom backs the car out, it hits something small, and Melody falls completely silent because she understands that something terrible has happened.
paragraphs.simple: Slowly, the big car rolled backward. Melody felt the car hit something with a soft thud. Then she became completely silent. She understood that something terrible had just happened.

paragraphs.context: but her voice said otherwise. For the first time I could remember,
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. V says Penny will be fine, but the sound of her voice shows she does not really believe it, and this is the first time Melody has ever heard her sound unsure.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. V says she is sure Penny will be just fine, but her voice tells a different story. For the first time that Melody can remember, Mrs. V sounds unsure of herself.

paragraphs.context: I don’t even know where I belong anymore.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody dreams of leaving the special classroom, yet she is not sure she belongs with the other fifth graders either; she no longer knows where she fits in.
paragraphs.simple: Melody then thinks about herself. She is the dreamer who tries to get out of room H-5. She is a kid whose computer is named Elvira. She no longer knows which group she is part of — where she belongs.

paragraphs.context: I don’t have the box with the picture on it.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody compares growing up to a puzzle without the picture on the box: she does not know what she is supposed to become, and she is not even sure she has all the pieces.
paragraphs.simple: Melody says life is like someone giving her a puzzle, but she does not have the box with the picture on it, so she does not know what the finished puzzle should look like. She is not even sure she has all the pieces. She adds that this may not be a good comparison, because she could not put a puzzle together even if she wanted to. Even though she usually knows the answers to most questions at school, many things in life still confuse her.

paragraphs.context: I’ve watched those things a million times
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody has watched videos of herself as a baby countless times, and the small details in them tell two quiet stories: her mother already sensed something was wrong, and Melody was never like a normal baby.
paragraphs.simple: Melody watches old home videos of herself as a baby again and again. In one picture, her mother is smiling, but her eyes are squeezed tight with worry — her mother already knew something was not right. In the other pictures, Melody sees how different she was from other babies: her arms and legs were very thin, she never kicked or splashed in the bath, and she almost never cried. Nobody says these things out loud in the videos. The pictures say them silently: a worried mother, and a baby who was never like other babies.

paragraphs.context: None of them can fix me, so I usually ignore them
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody understands the doctors perfectly well, but she deliberately performs the stupid, blank child they believe she is — because that is what they expect anyway.
paragraphs.simple: Melody has seen dozens of doctors, and they all study her like a puzzle. None of them can fix her, so she has learned a trick: she puts on an empty face, stares at one wall, and pretends their questions are too hard for her. It is all an act. She understands every word. But since the doctors have already decided she is mentally slow, she gives them exactly the show they expect. The last line is bitter, not sad: she is not failing their tests — she has stopped playing their game.

paragraphs.context: I know for a fact that all the animals he had pictured
paragraphs.mainIdea: The doctor’s test has a hidden trick — a cow’s, whale’s, camel’s, and elephant’s babies are ALL called calves — so Melody taps every picture, but the doctor marks her wrong anyway.
paragraphs.simple: The doctor shows Melody four pictures — a cow, a whale, a camel, an elephant — and asks which animal’s baby is called a calf. He expects the easy answer: the cow. But Melody knows more than he does: the babies of ALL four animals are called calves. So she carefully taps each picture, one by one, to answer “all of them.” The doctor does not understand. He mumbles “cow” and writes in his notes, convinced she failed. The joke is on him — and that is why the next line, “I thought doctors were supposed to be smart,” is sarcasm, not praise.

paragraphs.context: Sometimes when I look at Willy, though, I get the feeling
paragraphs.mainIdea: Willy, who cannot control his own noises, strains with all his strength to be quiet for a few minutes — like a swimmer holding his breath — and looks sad when he fails.
paragraphs.simple: Willy is another child in Melody’s class whose body makes noises he cannot stop. Sometimes Melody watches him close his eyes, screw up his face, and concentrate with all his might on being still and silent. For a few minutes, it works. Melody compares it to a swimmer coming up for air: staying quiet costs Willy as much effort as holding your breath underwater. Then he opens his eyes, the noises start all over again, and he always looks sad. The paragraph’s quiet point: more than anything, Willy wishes he could be quiet like other people — and he cannot.

paragraphs.context: Don’t get bogged down in all those touchy-feely words
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. V is sick of sentimental pity-talk about disabled children — she wants real teaching, not pretty words, and she promises Melody will learn.
paragraphs.simple: Melody’s father uses big, kind-sounding words like “reach her highest potential.” Mrs. V cuts him off with “Oh, gag me!” — she feels nauseous hearing that kind of talk. Her message: do not get stuck in soft, sentimental phrases from books about disabled kids. Those words change nothing. Then she replaces the pity-talk with a hard promise: Melody is a child who CAN learn, and she WILL learn, if she stays with Mrs. V. The paragraph is Mrs. V throwing away pretty words and offering work instead.

paragraphs.context: I pointed to need on my board, then to read
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody is trying to say “I need to learn to read,” but Mrs. V misunderstands and thinks Melody is showing off words she already knows — so Melody can only repeat “More.”
paragraphs.simple: Melody points to two words on her talking board: NEED, then READ. She means: I need someone to teach me real reading — not baby words. But Mrs. V hears it wrong. She answers, “I know you can read lots of words, Melody,” as if Melody were just showing off. They are talking past each other. Melody points again, and the only word she can add is “More. More. More.” — more words, more learning, more than this. She feels tears coming, because the one person trying to help her has missed what she really wants.

paragraphs.context: is sort of like a coat with the buttons done up
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody compares her disobedient body to a coat buttoned into the wrong holes — everything twisted and uncomfortable — except her two perfect thumbs.
paragraphs.simple: Melody says her thumbs are magic: they work perfectly, with no flaws. But the rest of her body is like a coat whose buttons have been pushed through the wrong holes. The coat still covers you, but everything pulls and twists and feels wrong. That is exactly how her body feels to live in — parts that will not obey her. She tosses it off as a joke (“Go figure”), but the picture is precise: a body that fits badly, like a badly buttoned coat, with only the thumbs coming out right.

paragraphs.context: I screamed because I hated stuff that was just plain stupid
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody’s screaming has three stacked causes, each deeper than the last: the work is insulting, she cannot say so, and she may never be able to say what she thinks.
paragraphs.simple: Melody explains her screaming, and it is not one reason but three, each one cutting deeper. First, she screamed because the classwork was babyish and insulting — she hated it. Second, she screeched because she cannot talk, so she could not simply tell the teacher to stop. Third, she cried because she faced the darkest truth: she might NEVER be able to tell anyone what she is really thinking. Each “because” opens a deeper room. In the end she is crying “like a two-year-old” — an eleven-year-old genius trapped making a toddler’s noise.

paragraphs.context: that yellow brick road had lost some of its magic glow
paragraphs.mainIdea: After her frightening fall, even her beloved Wizard of Oz has lost its magic — and imagining a wish from the Wizard, she realizes she already has brains, courage, and heart.
paragraphs.simple: Melody loves the movie The Wizard of Oz: a girl follows a yellow brick road to ask a wizard for wishes, and her three friends ask him for brains, a heart, and courage. But after Melody fell from her wheelchair and was badly scared, the movie feels empty — the yellow brick road has “lost its magic glow.” Still, she plays the wishing game: if the wizard blew her and her dog to Oz, what would they ask for? Brains? She has plenty. Courage? Her dog fears nothing. A heart? They both have lots of heart. So her only wish is small and sweet: to sing badly like the Cowardly Lion and dance badly like the Tin Man — just to do those things at all. She does not want to be fixed; she wants to be herself, only freer.

paragraphs.context: I realize I’ve been waiting for this thing all my life
paragraphs.mainIdea: The repeated “I wait.” builds the maddening slowness of the bureaucracy — and the last line doubles the meaning: she has waited her whole life to speak.
paragraphs.simple: Getting the talking machine takes forever: an online application, a doctor’s prescription (a prescription — for a MACHINE?), insurance approval, financial forms, a missing signature, one more school form. After every step, Melody writes the same two words: “I wait.” The repetition drums the frustration into you. Then comes the final line, and it lands twice: “I realize I’ve been waiting for this thing all my life.” She means the weeks of waiting for the machine — and she means her whole eleven years of waiting to speak at all.

paragraphs.context: Stupid elevator music floats from the tinny airport speakers
paragraphs.mainIdea: At her most hopeless moment, stranded at the airport, Melody’s synesthesia switches off: no colors in music, no smells — only darkness. Her private magic is gone.
paragraphs.simple: Through the whole book, Melody has had a secret gift: music gives her colors, sounds give her smells. But now, stranded at the airport with the trip destroyed, she squeezes her eyes shut and finds nothing. The cheap elevator music brings no beautiful colors. She smells no lovely aromas. All she can see is the darkness behind her eyelids. Her magic sense has shut down — and that silence tells you how deep her despair is: even the colors have abandoned her.

sentences.context: how I untangled the complicated process of words and thought
sentences.grammar: The words 'how I untangled the complicated process of words and thought' work together as one long object of 'I have no idea' — they say what she has no idea about.
sentences.simple: I do not know how I learned to understand words and thinking. But it happened fast and easily.

sentences.context: with feet sometimes kicking out unexpectedly and arms occasionally flailing
sentences.grammar: 'With feet kicking out and arms flailing' is a short way to show what her body is doing at the same time — 'with' plus a body part plus an -ing verb.
sentences.simple: Her feet sometimes kick out without warning, and her arms sometimes swing wildly and hit things near her.

sentences.context: “Jazz makes me itch,” she says with a frown
sentences.grammar: 'Makes me itch' means 'causes me to itch' — after 'me,' the verb 'itch' has no 'to.'
sentences.simple: Jazz music bothers Mom so much that it feels like an itch.

sentences.context: how the threads of a rug are woven as I lay there
sentences.grammar: 'Are woven' is passive — the threads do not weave themselves; someone weaves them. 'As I lay there' tells when it happened: at the same time.
sentences.simple: I had many chances to learn how a rug is made while I lay there waiting for someone to pick me up.

sentences.context: If I could switch places with you, I’d do it in a heartbeat
sentences.grammar: 'If I could ... I'd do' talks about something that cannot really happen — the 'if' part uses past tense ('could') and the result uses 'would' ('I'd').
sentences.simple: Dad says: if it were possible to trade places with you, I would do it right away.

sentences.context: I thought doctors were supposed to be smart
sentences.grammar: 'Were supposed to be' shows what people expect — doctors are expected to be smart.
sentences.simple: I believed that doctors should be smart. That was what people expected of them.

sentences.context: It takes time to accept the limitations of a beloved child
sentences.grammar: 'It' here has no real meaning — the real subject is the long 'to accept...' part at the end. The sentence says: accepting this takes time.
sentences.simple: A parent needs time before she can accept that her loved child has limits.

sentences.context: Melody will never be able to walk on her own or speak
sentences.grammar: Two verb phrases share 'be able to': (1) walk on her own, (2) speak a sentence. 'On her own' means without help.
sentences.simple: She will never learn to walk without help, and she will never learn to say even one sentence.

sentences.context: so I can spell out words, and a row of numbers under that
sentences.grammar: 'So I can ...' shows purpose — why the letters and numbers are there. Two 'so' parts match two tools: letters for spelling, numbers for counting.
sentences.simple: There is a line of letters at the top so I can spell words, and a line of numbers below it so I can count, say how many, or talk about time.

sentences.context: She let me fall out of my wheelchair onto pillows so I could learn
sentences.grammar: After 'let me,' the verb 'fall' has no 'to' — 'let' is always followed by a plain verb. 'So I could learn' gives the reason.
sentences.simple: She let me fall from my chair onto soft pillows so I could learn how to stop my own falls.

sentences.context: If I have to sit five more minutes in this traffic jam
sentences.grammar: In an 'if' sentence about the future, the 'if' part uses present tense ('have to sit') while the result uses 'will' ('I'll explode').
sentences.simple: If I must sit five more minutes in this traffic jam, I will feel like exploding.

sentences.context: Either because of the time out of the bowl or because
sentences.grammar: 'Either A or B' gives two possible reasons before the main news. The main news ('Ollie didn't survive') comes last, after the comma.
sentences.simple: Ollie died for one of two reasons: he was out of the bowl too long, or the new water was not the right temperature.

sentences.context: because my head was pulsing with the things I wanted to
sentences.simple: Suddenly I could not hear him anymore, because so many unsaid words were beating hard inside my head.
sentences.grammar: “The things I wanted to say but couldn’t” leaves out the last word — “but couldn’t [say them]”; “my head was pulsing” is a picture for words pushing to get out.

sentences.context: Right. I’ll get to potty training tonight—on the twenty-fifth hour
sentences.simple: Mom is joking: she will do potty training in “the twenty-fifth hour” — a time that does not exist, because a day has only 24 hours. She means she has no time at all.
sentences.grammar: A day has only 24 hours, so “the twenty-fifth hour” is a joke meaning “never” — Mom is saying she is far too busy, and she does not really mean it.

sentences.context: but all that comes out are meaningless sounds and squeaks.
sentences.simple: I have many words in my head, but only sounds with no meaning come out of my mouth.
sentences.grammar: “All that comes out” means “the only thing that comes out” — here “all” points to the small, sad result, not to a large amount.

sentences.context: It was driving me crazy that I couldn’t tell him about
sentences.simple: I was feeling very bad because I could not tell him that I wanted a Big Mac.
sentences.grammar: “It” does not point to a thing here — “It was driving me crazy that...” means “The fact that I couldn’t tell him was making me lose control.”

sentences.context: And because he’s one of the popular kids, and probably the
sentences.simple: Connor is popular and big, so when he says Melody's computer is awesome, the other kids stop making fun of it.
sentences.grammar: The sentence puts two reasons together with “because... and...”: Connor is popular, Connor is big — and, Melody thinks, when he says it is good, the others stop.

sentences.context: Well, it’s gotta be short. What can you do in eleven
sentences.simple: Connor jokes that the life story must be short, because an eleven-year-old has not lived long enough to have much to write about.
sentences.grammar: Connor is not really asking a question here; he means “Not much can happen in eleven years.”

sentences.context: Red-bronze leaves. Bright gold sunlight. Leftover summer.
sentences.simple: It is a beautiful early-November day: the leaves are red and bronze, the sunlight is bright and gold, and it still feels a little like summer.
sentences.grammar: These are not full sentences — just short word-pictures with no verbs, listing what the beautiful day looks like.

sentences.context: come the two people I’d least want to run into: Molly
sentences.simple: Then Molly and Claire — the two people Melody least wants to meet — come around the corner.
sentences.grammar: The sentence turns the normal word order around: “come the two people” puts the action word before the people, which makes it feel sudden and strong when they come.

sentences.context: she thanks us properly and says she had a real good
sentences.simple: Rose thanks them in a nice and careful way and says she had a really good time — but Melody's next line, “But did she?”, shows she is not sure Rose really means it.
sentences.grammar: “But did she?” is not a real question — it means “Did she really?”, showing Melody is not sure Rose means her nice words.

sentences.context: and Rose has the Internet—I guess that means the whole
sentences.simple: I still point to words taped to a board on my wheelchair, but Rose has the whole Internet — almost the whole world of knowledge — ready to use.
sentences.grammar: The sentence joins two different pictures with “and”: her poor old board against Rose's big world of knowledge; the short lines (—) hold her sad words in the middle.

sentences.context: I’ve heard of prescriptions for antibiotics, but for machines? That seems
sentences.simple: I know doctors give prescriptions for medicine, but a prescription for a machine? That sounds crazy.
sentences.grammar: Words are left out the second time: “but for machines?” means “but [a prescription] for machines?” — the question mark shows she does not believe it.

sentences.context: sometimes it’s good to have something that nobody else knows but
sentences.simple: Naming the machine is probably silly, but it is nice to have a secret that only you know.
sentences.grammar: “But” here means “except”: “something that nobody else knows but you” is a secret that nobody knows except you.

sentences.context: I know you feel like a ton of bricks have been
sentences.simple: I know you feel free and happy, as if a very heavy weight has been taken off you.
sentences.grammar: “Like a ton of bricks have been lifted” is a picture: a huge heavy weight taken away stands for the end of years of not speaking.

sentences.context: in a voice that sounded like he’d been chewing on dry
sentences.simple: One afternoon near the end of January, Mr. Dimming said in a dry, hard voice: instead of class, they would have a practice round for the quiz team.
sentences.grammar: The words about his voice sit in the middle of the sentence; take them out and the main line is “Mr. Dimming announced: Instead of regular class today, we’ll have a practice round.”

sentences.context: If Melody Brooks can win the first round, then my questions
sentences.simple: Mr. Dimming means: if even Melody could win, my questions were too easy — which makes her win sound like a bad thing.
sentences.grammar: “If X can win, then Y must be true”: he uses her win as proof that the questions were easy, so his kind words really hurt her.

sentences.context: Penny was used to things falling off my chair
sentences.simple: Things often fell off Melody’s chair, so Penny felt this was normal and did not know Melody was being mean on purpose.
sentences.grammar: “Was used to” before a verb like “falling” means the action felt normal because it happened often. It is not the same as “used to” + verb, which talks about the past.

sentences.context: while I pulled the cards that I’d knocked down into a messy pile
sentences.simple: While I pulled the cards — the ones I had knocked down — into a messy pile on the floor.
sentences.grammar: “That I’d knocked down” tells which cards; “that” stands for “which” and “I’d” is “I had.”

sentences.context: I had the info stuck in my head
sentences.simple: The facts stayed in my head; I remembered them.
sentences.grammar: “Had the info stuck” shows a result: the info was stuck in her head. “Have + thing + done” tells what happened to the thing, not who did it.

sentences.context: that Tokyo was the capital of Japan, Addis Ababa the capital of Ethiopia
sentences.simple: I answered that Tokyo was the capital of Japan, that Addis Ababa was the capital of Ethiopia, and so on for Canada and Colombia.
sentences.grammar: After the first pair, “was the capital of” is left out but still understood — the list gives four answers in short form.

sentences.context: Deleted the memory—need room for facts
sentences.simple: I deleted the bad memory. I need room in my head for facts.
sentences.grammar: The “I” is left out twice to sound fast and cool: the full form is “I deleted the memory — I need room for facts.”

sentences.context: warm February days that fools the hyacinths into thinking spring is here
sentences.simple: Warm days in February trick the flowers, so the flowers believe spring has come.
sentences.grammar: “Fool someone into thinking” = trick them so they believe. The “into thinking” part shows the result.

sentences.context: Afraid it would feel so good, I’d just fly away
sentences.simple: I was afraid that flying would feel so good that I would just fly away and never come back.
sentences.grammar: “I was” is left out at the start: the full form is “I was afraid (that) it would feel so good (that) I’d just fly away.”

sentences.context: these cookies must have been made in chocolate heaven
sentences.simple: These cookies are so good that they seem to come from a heaven made of chocolate.
sentences.grammar: “Must have been made” guesses about the past: she feels sure they were made in a wonderful place — a joke, since no such place is real.

sentences.context: Boy, does our big old car need a trip to the car wash!
sentences.simple: Our big old car really needs to go to the car wash!
sentences.grammar: The word order is flipped for strong feeling: the normal order is “Our big old car really needs a trip to the car wash!” “Boy” starts the cry of surprise.

sentences.context: as fast as her short little legs will carry her, she bolts for Dad
sentences.simple: She runs to Dad at the highest speed her short little legs allow.
sentences.grammar: “As fast as” plus a group of words sets the top speed: she ran as fast as her legs could carry her — no faster was possible.

sentences.context: I thought about it, then decided not to
sentences.simple: I thought about telling Rose, then decided not to tell her.
sentences.grammar: “Not to” stands for the whole verb phrase “not to tell Rose” — the verb is left out because the last sentence already said it.

sentences.context: I hold in my hand the official test questions
sentences.simple: I am holding the real test questions in my hand.
sentences.grammar: The normal order is “I hold the official test questions in my hand” — the place part moves to the front to sound big and important.

sentences.context: He’s looking right over my head at Catherine, as if I were invisible
sentences.simple: He looks past me at Catherine, as if I were not there at all.
sentences.grammar: “As if I were” imagines something untrue — she IS there. “Were” (not “was”) is used for unreal situations.

sentences.context: Us normal people aren’t allowed to use computers
sentences.simple: We normal people are not allowed to use computers.
sentences.grammar: By the rules, the subject should be “We normal people,” but in normal talk people say “us” — the book keeps Claire’s real, rude voice.

sentences.context: I’m amazed she’s been able to achieve as well as she has
sentences.simple: I am amazed that she has been able to do so well.
sentences.grammar: “As well as she has” = as well as she has achieved — the verb “achieved” is left out after the second “as.”

sentences.context: Don’t you mean when we stomp the competition?
sentences.simple: Don’t you mean “when we beat the other teams badly”? We will win for sure.
sentences.grammar: Claire changes “if” to “when”: “if” shows doubt, but “when” shows she is sure they will win.

sentences.context: If classroom behavior were a determining factor for making the team
sentences.simple: If good behavior in class decided who gets on the team (but it does not)...
sentences.grammar: “Were” (not “was”) imagines an unreal situation: behavior does NOT decide, but if it did, Connor would be in trouble.

sentences.context: Two fifth graders. Two from sixth grade.
sentences.simple: Two of the alternates are fifth graders. Two are from sixth grade.
sentences.grammar: Short pieces stand for full sentences: “Two (are) fifth graders. Two (are) from sixth grade.” The verb “are” is left out in the fast list of names.

sentences.context: To know all the finalists are from fifth grade blows me away
sentences.simple: Learning that all four winners are from fifth grade surprises me very much.
sentences.grammar: The long “To know...” part is the subject of “blows”: knowing this fact is what surprises him.

sentences.context: I try not to kick and drip and make my teammates sorry
sentences.simple: I try not to kick, not to drip, and not to make my teammates feel sorry about me.
sentences.grammar: Three verbs share one “try not to”: try not to kick, (not to) drip, (not to) make — “to” is said once but works for all three.

sentences.context: The more I think about it, the more excited I get
sentences.simple: When I think about it more, I get more excited.
sentences.grammar: The “the more... the more...” shape joins two growing things: more thinking brings more excitement.

sentences.context: I showed up at practice on Wednesday afternoon as if nothing had happened
sentences.simple: I came to practice on Wednesday as if the strange moment on Tuesday had never happened.
sentences.grammar: “As if” + “had happened” (past perfect) imagines a past that is not true: something DID happen on Tuesday.

sentences.context: it took me too long to spell out the word
sentences.simple: I needed too much time to spell the word.
sentences.grammar: The shape is “it takes (someone) (time) to do (something)”: it took me too much time to spell out the word.

sentences.context: “TV makes lots of people look funny,” I had the machine say
sentences.simple: I made my talker say that television makes lots of people look funny — maybe even you, Claire.
sentences.grammar: “Had the machine say” = I caused the machine to say it. “Have + thing + verb” shows she made it happen.

sentences.context: Rose’s mom ordered pizza for everyone and had it delivered to the school
sentences.simple: Rose’s mom ordered pizza for everyone and asked someone to bring it to the school.
sentences.grammar: “Had it delivered” = she caused it to be delivered by someone else. “Have + thing + done” means another person does the work.

sentences.context: I’ll go get a slice for you
sentences.simple: I will get a slice of pizza for you.
sentences.grammar: “Go get” puts two verbs together: “go” only shows movement; the real action is “get.”

sentences.context: How could I explain to her that without Catherine or my mom
sentences.simple: I could not explain to her that I cannot eat without Catherine, Mom, or Mrs. V to feed me.
sentences.grammar: A question that expects no answer: she means “I could not explain it.” “How could I...?” shows it was impossible.

sentences.context: is a little too heavy for Mom to handle on her own
sentences.simple: is so heavy that Mom cannot lift it by herself.
sentences.grammar: “Too heavy for Mom to handle” = so heavy that Mom cannot handle it. The shape is “too” + word + “for” + person + “to” + verb.

sentences.context: And here, Miss Melody, is where you will sit
sentences.simple: And you will sit here, Miss Melody.
sentences.grammar: The normal order is “Where you will sit is here” — “here” jumps to the front because Paul is pointing at the place.

sentences.context: My mom made me wear this tie
sentences.simple: My mom forced me to wear this tie.
sentences.grammar: “Made me wear” = she forced it. After “make” we use the verb with no “to”: wear, not “to wear.”

sentences.context: If he does, at least the attention will be on him instead of me
sentences.simple: If he chokes on live TV, at least people will watch him and not me.
sentences.grammar: “If he does” = if he chokes — the verb is left out because the last sentence already said “choke.”

sentences.context: Claire says loud enough for me to hear
sentences.simple: Claire says it so loudly that I can hear it.
sentences.grammar: “Loud enough for me to hear” = so loud that I could hear it. The shape is “enough” + “for” + person + “to” + verb.

sentences.context: No way am I letting their negativity mess me up
sentences.simple: I will not let their mean talk hurt me in any way.
sentences.grammar: “No way” at the front flips the order for force: the normal order is “I am not letting their negativity mess me up in any way.”

sentences.context: a slim guy with hair that looks like it has been glued into place
sentences.simple: a thin man. His hair looks as if someone glued it in place.
sentences.grammar: The extra part says “the moderator”: it adds words with no new “is” — “a slim guy...” means “who is a slim guy.”

sentences.context: will meet for what we call a ‘quiz-off,’
sentences.simple: will meet for the final round, the thing we name a “quiz-off.”
sentences.grammar: “What we call a quiz-off” = the thing that we name “quiz-off.” “What” stands for “the thing that.”

sentences.context: this is not a test of speed, but of accuracy
sentences.simple: This is not a test of speed. It is a test of being correct.
sentences.grammar: “Not a test of speed, but of accuracy”: “a test” is said once and works for both parts — not (a test) of speed, but (a test) of accuracy.

sentences.context: Two people on the Woodland team answered “hurricane” instead
sentences.simple: Two Woodland students answered “hurricane” instead of the right answer, “earthquake.”
sentences.grammar: “Instead” = instead of the right answer — the words after “instead of” are left out because we know the question.

sentences.context: I never thought about what teachers dream about
sentences.simple: I never thought about the things that teachers dream about.
sentences.grammar: “What teachers dream about” is the thing she never thought about. The sentence ends with “about” because “what” moved to the front.

sentences.context: a check for two thousand dollars to be used for academic endeavors
sentences.simple: a check for two thousand dollars. The school will use it for school work.
sentences.grammar: “To be used for...” tells the check’s purpose: the check will be used (by the school), not the check using something.

sentences.context: OMG! What a night! I still can’t believe how everything turned out
sentences.simple: Oh my God! What an amazing night! I still cannot believe what happened.
sentences.grammar: “What a night!” = what an amazing night. “What a” + noun shows very strong feeling.

sentences.context: Even though Connor aced a hard spelling problem and Claire came through
sentences.simple: Connor did very well on spelling, and Claire did very well on history. But even so, Perry Valley stayed ahead.
sentences.grammar: “Even though” starts a surprise: two good things happened, BUT the other team still stayed one or two points ahead.

sentences.context: Not only was it one of Mrs. V’s vocabulary words, it was me!
sentences.simple: It was not only a word Mrs. V taught her. The question described Melody herself.
sentences.grammar: “Not only” at the front flips the order: the normal order is “It was not only one of the words Mrs. V taught; it was me.”

sentences.context: It could have been C, but it might have been D
sentences.simple: The answer was possibly C, but it was possibly D. She had to choose.
sentences.grammar: “Could have been” talks about a past possibility: C was possible, but in the end she chose D.

sentences.context: Either we were all correct or all really terrible at figuring out time problems
sentences.simple: Two choices: either our whole team was right, or our whole team was very bad at time problems.
sentences.grammar: “Either A or B” gives two choices: (either) we were all correct, or (we were) all terrible — words are left out the second time.

sentences.context: I missed a few on purpose so the other contestants wouldn’t feel bad
sentences.simple: I chose to miss a few, so the other students would not feel bad. (A joke — he really just missed them.)
sentences.grammar: “On purpose” = he chose to do it; “so... wouldn’t” tells the kind reason. It is a joke: he did not miss them on purpose at all.

sentences.context: “How about Linguini’s?” Connor suggested. “They’ve got all-you-can-eat spaghetti.”
sentences.simple: Connor suggests the restaurant Linguini’s, which lets you eat as much spaghetti as you want.
sentences.grammar: “How about...?” suggests an idea. It is not a real question about “how” — it means “Let’s try this.”

sentences.context: “Well, I wouldn’t go that far,” Molly said, glancing at Claire.
sentences.simple: Molly does not fully agree: she would not say something that strong.
sentences.grammar: “Wouldn’t go that far” = would not agree that much. “Go that far” pictures agreement as a road — she stops before the end.

sentences.context: Connor’s dad, the last to go up, looked at me
sentences.simple: The dad went up the steps last. He looked at me, then at the steps.
sentences.grammar: “The last to go up” = who went up last. After “the first/last,” “who went” can be left out.

sentences.context: Pull. Roll up. Bump. First step.
sentences.simple: Mom pulls the chair, rolls it up, and bumps over the first stone step.
sentences.grammar: Each step up gets three short orders and a count. The very short pieces make you feel every hard pull and bump.

sentences.context: Only my mom would order baked fish at an Italian restaurant!
sentences.simple: My mom is the only person who would order baked fish at an Italian restaurant!
sentences.grammar: “Would” here shows what is normal for Mom: of course SHE would do this strange thing. Nobody else would.

sentences.context: all I wanted to do was go home
sentences.simple: The only thing I wanted was to go home.
sentences.grammar: “All I wanted” is the subject: the thing I wanted was to go home. “All” = the only thing.

sentences.context: I saw Molly poke Claire, and they exchanged looks
sentences.simple: I watched Molly poke Claire, and then they looked at each other in a knowing way.
sentences.grammar: After “see,” we use the verb with no “to”: I saw (Molly) poke. She watched the action happen.

sentences.context: Claire gets sick in the middle of a crowded restaurant, yet I’m the one
sentences.simple: Claire got sick in a full restaurant, but I am the one people stare at.
sentences.grammar: “Yet” joins two surprising facts: Claire did the embarrassing thing, BUT I get the strange looks.

sentences.context: You skip a practice and you get bounced to the alternates
sentences.grammar: Two short orders joined by “and” work like an “if” sentence: “You skip … and you get …” means “If you skip, you will get …”.
sentences.simple: If you miss even one practice, you will lose your place on the team and become an alternate. I am in this to win.

sentences.context: that the storm system will have fizzled by then
sentences.grammar: “will have fizzled” is the future perfect tense: it describes something that will already be finished at a later time.
sentences.simple: The weather service says the storm will already have died out by then, so planes can start taking people where they need to go.

sentences.context: It’s a good thing they did too, or they wouldn’t have gotten out.
sentences.grammar: “or they wouldn’t have gotten out” imagines the opposite past: without going early, they would have been stuck too.
sentences.simple: It is lucky that they went to the airport early. If they had not, their flight would have been cancelled too, and they could not have left.

sentences.context: The word is WAS. There is no IS.
sentences.grammar: The one-word sentence “Was.” and the shouted “WAS” / “IS” use past and present tense alone to say Melody is out: she WAS on the team, she IS not.
sentences.simple: Mom means Melody WAS the brightest person on the team, but she is not on the team anymore — there is no “is” now.

sentences.context: And the mad me decided that I was not going to sit at home
sentences.grammar: “the mad me” puts the adjective “mad” before “me” to mean “the angry part of me,” not the whole person.
sentences.simple: And the angry part of me decided that I would not sit at home like a dog that people kick around.

sentences.context: We’re gonna clean Doodle up and have him waiting for Penny
sentences.grammar: “have him waiting” uses have + person + -ing to mean “make sure he is in that state”: they will arrange for Doodle to be waiting.
sentences.simple: We are going to wash Doodle and make sure he is clean and waiting when Penny comes home.

sentences.context: Your head must be near ’bout ready to explode
sentences.grammar: “’bout” is short for “about” in casual speech, and “ready to explode” is a joke: so much has happened that her head feels full to bursting.
sentences.simple: After everything that has happened in the past few days, your head must feel like it is about to burst.

sentences.context: How can silence be so loud?
sentences.grammar: A question that expects no answer: “loud silence” joins two opposite words to show how shocking the quiet feels.
sentences.simple: The quiet in the room feels shocking and heavy, as if the silence itself were making a noise.

sentences.context: each one delicate and different, each one melting untouched in my hands
sentences.grammar: The two short word groups after the dash have no verb; they just paint a picture of the snowflakes — and of the words.
